tracks.name: API Contracts
tracks.description: Interfaces that survive real clients, retries and time.

lessons.title: 1. Pagination as a contract
lessons.summary: Return a shape that tells the client how to ask for the next page.

activities.title: Data plus a way forward
activities.instruction: A bare array forces the client to guess the page size and append `?page=` forever. Return an envelope with the page and an opaque cursor for the next one. The cursor hides how pagination works, so you can change the strategy later without breaking clients.

activities.title: Offset drift
activities.question: A client is on `page=2` of an offset-paginated feed when three new posts are inserted at the top. What happens on the next request?
choices: Some posts appear twice and none are missing
Nothing changes — offsets are stable
The request fails with a 409
activities.answer: Some posts appear twice and none are missing
activities.explanation: The offset counted rows from the old start. New rows shift everything down, so page 2 now begins with rows the user already saw.

activities.title: Return an envelope
activities.instruction: Return `{ data, nextCursor }` from the route, using the last row's id when there is another page.

teaching.text: Clients break on shapes, not on intentions. Decide the envelope, the page size cap and the end-of-list signal once, then keep them.
res.json({ data: page, nextCursor: hasMore ? page.at(-1)._id : null });
Cap `limit`. An uncapped page size is a denial-of-service waiting for one curious client.

lessons.task: Return data with a nextCursor for the next page.
hints: Fetch one extra row to know whether a next page exists.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does an opaque cursor make future pagination changes easier?

lessons.title: 2. Idempotent writes
lessons.summary: If a client can retry, the write must be safe to repeat.

activities.title: One key, one charge
activities.instruction: Networks time out and clients retry. A charge that ran server-side but timed out will run again on retry, unless the request carries a key the server remembers. Store the key with the result, return the stored result on repeat, and let a unique index enforce it.

activities.title: The timeout retry
activities.question: The server charges the card, then the response times out. The client retries without an idempotency key. What is the outcome?
choices: A second charge, because the server cannot tell it is a retry
The first charge is refunded automatically
The retry is rejected as a duplicate
activities.answer: A second charge, because the server cannot tell it is a retry
activities.explanation: At-least-once delivery is the normal case, not the exception. Idempotency moves duplicate detection to the server, where it can be enforced.

activities.title: Make the charge safe to retry
activities.instruction: Read `Idempotency-Key`, return the stored result when it exists, and store it after charging.

teaching.text: Idempotency is not caching. The guarantee is that repeating the same request has the same effect as doing it once; the response should be the original one.

const existing = await Payment.findOne({ idempotencyKey: key });
if (existing) return res.status(200).json(existing.result);
Two racing retries can both pass the find check. A unique index on the key turns that race into a duplicate-key error you can handle.

lessons.task: Make the payment route idempotent using the Idempotency-Key header.
hints: Look the key up before charging, and save it with the result.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is a unique database index needed even when you check for the key first?

lessons.title: 3. Errors and versioning
lessons.summary: Give every failure a code, a message and a request id.

activities.title: One error shape
activities.instruction: Clients branch on status codes and stable machine-readable codes, not on prose. One error middleware, one shape, and a request id in every response so a user's screenshot can be traced to a log line.

activities.title: Which change is breaking?
activities.question: Which API change is most likely to break existing clients?
choices: Renaming `userName` to `username` in responses
Adding a new optional field to a response
Adding a new endpoint
activities.explanation: Additive changes are usually safe. Renames and removals break parsing. Version when you must; keep the old shape until clients migrate.

activities.title: Write the error middleware
activities.instruction: Return one error shape with `code`, a safe `message` and `requestId` from `req.id`, hiding the message for 500s.

teaching.text: An error contract is part of the API. Decide the codes and statuses once, write them down, and let the client show copy based on the code.
Never forward a raw database or stack-trace message to a client. Log it with the request id; return the id instead.

lessons.task: Write an error middleware with a stable error shape.
hints: Use `err.status` for the status and `req.id` for the id.

const status = err.status || 500;
res.status(status).json({ error: { code: err.code || 'internal_error', message, requestId: req.id } });
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why do clients prefer a stable error code over a readable message?

tracks.name: Queues & Caching
tracks.description: Move slow work out of the request and keep hot data close.

lessons.title: 4. Background jobs
lessons.summary: Anything that can take seconds belongs outside the request.

activities.title: Respond, then work
activities.instruction: Sending email, generating PDFs and calling third parties inside a request ties your latency and availability to theirs. Enqueue a job and return. Workers retry with backoff, so job handlers must be idempotent.

activities.title: Why not inline?
activities.question: What is the main reason not to call a third-party email API directly inside the signup request?
choices: The request inherits the provider's latency and failures
Emails cannot be sent from an HTTP handler
The API key would be exposed to the user
activities.answer: The request inherits the provider's latency and failures
activities.explanation: A slow provider makes signup slow; a down provider makes signup fail. A queue decouples your success from theirs.

activities.title: Enqueue the email
activities.instruction: Replace the awaited send with `emailQueue.add('welcome', ...)` using retry attempts, then respond 202.

teaching.text: Queues turn a synchronous dependency into a boundary. The request does the minimum durable work, and the worker can be retried, scaled and paused independently.
Retries mean your handler will run more than once. Use the job id or a unique business key so a retried job does not send two receipts.

lessons.task: Queue the welcome email instead of awaiting it.
hints: Add the job to the queue and return before it runs.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why must a job handler tolerate running twice?

lessons.title: 5. Caching with Redis
lessons.summary: Read from the cache, fall back to the database, invalidate on write.

activities.title: Cache by identity, expire by time
activities.instruction: The cache-aside pattern reads the cache first, loads from the database on a miss, and stores the result with a TTL. Writes must delete the key, or users keep seeing stale data until it expires. Always key by the identity the response depends on.

activities.title: The shared key
activities.question: A profile endpoint caches the response under the key `profile` for all users. What happens?
choices: One user's private profile is served to everyone else
The cache hit rate drops to zero
Redis rejects the second write
activities.answer: One user's private profile is served to everyone else
activities.explanation: The key is the cache's identity. If it does not include the user, the cache stops distinguishing users — a data leak and a correctness bug at once.

activities.title: Write the cache-aside read
activities.instruction: Write `getUser(id)`: read `user:${id}` from Redis, fall back to the database, cache for 300 seconds, and delete the key in `updateUser`.

teaching.text: A cache is a copy you can afford to lose. That means the database stays the source of truth, every cached value has an expiry, and writes know which keys they invalidate.
Avoid caching per-user data on a shared CDN. Redis is private and keyed; a public edge cache is not.

lessons.task: Implement cache-aside for a user lookup and invalidate on update.
hints: Build the key from the user id in both functions.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is a cache without a TTL a correctness bug waiting to happen?

lessons.title: 6. Rate limiting
lessons.summary: Protect the service and tell the client when to come back.

activities.title: Count per window, per identity
activities.instruction: A fixed-window counter is the simplest limiter: increment a key, set an expiry on the first hit, and reject once the count passes the limit. Key it by user or IP and return 429 with `Retry-After` so well-behaved clients back off instead of hammering.

activities.title: The window edge
activities.question: A fixed window of 100 requests per minute resets at :00. A client sends 100 at :59 and 100 at :01. What does the limiter allow?
choices: 200 requests in a two-second span
100 in total
The second batch is queued
activities.explanation: Fixed windows allow double bursts at the boundary. A sliding window or token bucket smooths this; the simple counter is still a reasonable first step.

activities.title: Implement the limiter
activities.instruction: Increment a per-user key with `incr`, set an `expire`, and respond 429 when the count exceeds the limit.

teaching.text: Rate limiting is both protection and a product decision. Limits per user, per IP and per endpoint answer different attacks; start with the expensive ones.
An in-process limiter counts per instance. Behind a load balancer that means N times the intended limit — use a shared store.

lessons.task: Write a Redis-backed fixed-window limiter returning 429.
hints: `INCR` creates the key at 1; set the expiry only on that first increment.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does a limiter kept in memory stop working when you add a second server?

tracks.name: Scaling Decisions
tracks.description: What changes when one server becomes many.

lessons.title: 7. Stateless services
lessons.summary: Any instance must be able to serve any request.

activities.title: Local memory is not shared
activities.instruction: In-memory sessions, uploads written to disk and per-process caches all assume one server. Behind a load balancer the next request may land elsewhere. Move state into Redis, the database or object storage so instances are interchangeable.

activities.title: Two instances
activities.question: A service keeps rate-limit counters in module memory and runs two instances. Each enforces 100 requests per minute. What is the effective limit?
choices: 200 per minute, split across whichever instance answers
100 per minute, because they share memory
50 per minute
activities.answer: 200 per minute, split across whichever instance answers
activities.explanation: Each process counts only what it saw. Any state that must be globally true needs a shared store.

activities.title: Move sessions out
activities.instruction: Configure express-session to use a Redis store instead of the default in-memory store.

teaching.text: Statelessness is a property you choose: no request depends on what a previous request left in this process's memory. It is what makes restarts and horizontal scaling boring.
app.use(session({ store: new RedisStore({ client: redis }), ... }));
Uploads are state too. Write to object storage and pass a URL, not a path on one machine's disk.

lessons.task: Switch the session store to Redis.
hints: Import the Redis store adapter and pass it as `store`.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does a local disk upload break the moment you run two instances?

lessons.title: 8. Replicas and read-your-writes
lessons.summary: A replica is behind by milliseconds — sometimes more.

activities.title: Route the read that matters
activities.instruction: Read replicas take load off the primary, but replication is asynchronous. A user who just saved a change may hit a replica that has not caught up. Send reads that must reflect the user's own write to the primary, or keep a short window after a write where the session reads primary.

activities.title: The vanished edit
activities.question: A user saves a new display name and is redirected to their profile, which reads from a replica. What do they see?
choices: The old name, until replication catches up
A database error
The new name, because writes replicate instantly
activities.answer: The old name, until replication catches up
activities.explanation: Replication is usually asynchronous. This is the 'read-your-writes' problem, and it looks like data loss to the user even though nothing was lost.

activities.title: Route the critical read
activities.instruction: Write `readerFor(user)` that returns the primary when the last write was under two seconds ago, otherwise the replica.

teaching.text: Replication buys read capacity at the cost of consistency. Decide per query: a product listing can be slightly stale, a bank balance after a transfer cannot.

const justWrote = Date.now() - user.lastWriteAt < 2000;
return justWrote ? primary : replicaPool.reader();
Measure replica lag and alert on it. A replica that falls minutes behind is a correctness incident, not a performance chart.

lessons.task: Route reads to the primary right after a write.
hints: Compare `Date.now()` with the stored last-write timestamp.

const justWrote = Date.now() - user.lastWriteAt < 2000;
return justWrote ? primary : replicaPool.reader();
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is 'the user just wrote' a better signal than 'always read the primary'?

lessons.title: 9. Write the trade-off down
lessons.summary: The most valuable design document is a short record of why.

activities.title: Context, decision, consequences
activities.instruction: An ADR is a one-page note kept next to the code: the situation, the choice, and what you accept by making it. It takes ten minutes and saves the next engineer from re-litigating a decision — or from unknowingly depending on it.
activities.example:
# Use Redis for session storage

## Context
Sessions live in process memory, so a second instance and every deploy log users out.

## Decision
Store sessions in Redis, which is already used for rate limiting.

## Consequences
- Sessions survive deploys and are shared across instances.
- Redis becomes a required dependency for login.
- A Redis outage logs everyone out; it is monitored with a pager.

activities.title: When is an ADR worth it?
activities.question: Which decision most deserves a written record?
choices: Adding a queue that the whole signup flow now depends on
Renaming a local variable
Adding a unit test
activities.answer: Adding a queue that the whole signup flow now depends on
activities.explanation: Write down decisions that are expensive to reverse or easy to misunderstand. Cheap, local, reversible choices do not need ceremony.

activities.title: Draft the ADR
activities.instruction: Write an ADR for adopting Redis, with Context, Decision and Consequences sections.

teaching.text: Architecture is a series of trade-offs, and each one has a cost you will pay later. Writing it down makes the cost explicit while you are still choosing.

## Context
## Decision
## Consequences
Put ADRs in the repository (`docs/adr/0007-redis-sessions.md`). A document in a wiki nobody opens is a decision nobody can find.

lessons.task: Write a short ADR for using Redis for sessions.
hints: Three headings, a few lines each. Name the cost in Consequences.

## Context
Sessions are lost on every deploy.

## Decision
Store sessions in Redis.

## Consequences
- Sessions survive deploys.
- Redis becomes a required dependency.
lessons.solution:
# Use Redis for session storage

## Context
Sessions live in process memory, so a second instance and every deploy log users out.

## Decision
Store sessions in Redis, which is already used for rate limiting.

## Consequences
- Sessions survive deploys and are shared across instances.
- Redis becomes a required dependency for login.
- A Redis outage logs everyone out; it is monitored with a pager.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is naming the downside the most useful line in an ADR?
